# 1.Magic Squares

A magic square is a square grid of usually positive natural numbers whose sums of the numbers in each row, column, and diagonals are the same.  
Here are a few examples,

![the famous one](magic_square1.png)

$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
17 & 113 & 47 \\ \hline
89 & 59 & 29 \\ \hline
71 & 5 & 101
\end{array}
$$  
This one is made of primes. It's sum is 177
 
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
7 & 12 & 1 & 14 \\ \hline
2 & 13 & 8 & 11 \\ \hline
16 & 3 & 10 & 5 \\ \hline
9 & 6 & 15 & 4
\end{array}
$$  
This one is 4 by 4 and sums to 34

# 2.Magic square of squares
A magic square is a magic square of square if the numbers in each cell can be squared and the resulting grid is also a magic square.  
No 3 by 3 magic square of squares has been found, but other magic square of squares have been.

Here's one found by Euler. Its sum is 8,515.
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
68^{2} & 29^{2} & 41^{2} & 37^{2} \\ \hline
17^{2} & 31^{2} & 79^{2} & 32^{2} \\ \hline
59^{2} & 28^{2} & 23^{2} & 61^{2} \\ \hline
11^{2} & 77^{2} & 8^{2} & 49^{2}
\end{array}
$$  

# 3. The Most General Case

A magic square is just a grid of numbers that match a certain criterion, so a kind of most general square can be constructed.
For the sake of breavity(and the ease of writing them in quarto) I'll write them in a matrix and use matrix notation instead of a grid or an array.  
So, a magic square can be written as a matrix of natural numbers.
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
a_{11} & a_{21} & \cdots & a_{1n} \\
a_{12} & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{1n} \\
\vdots & \vdots &\ddots & \vdots \\
a_{n1} & a_{n2} &\cdots & a_{nn}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Such that for some function $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $g:
\mathbb{N}^{n} \to \mathbb{N}$ suitably applying f then g to the matrix the
rows, columns, and diagonals evaluate to some single value $S$.
\begin{align*}
&g(f(a_{i1}), f(a_{i2}), \cdots, f(a_{in}))\ (1 \leq i \leq n) \\
= &g(f(a_{1j}), f(a_{2j}), \cdots, f(a_{nj}))\ (1 \leq j \leq n) \\
= &g(f(a_{11}), f(a_{22}), \cdots, f(a_{nn}))\\
= &g(f(a_{1n}), f(a_{2n-1}), \cdots, f(a_{n1}))\\
= &S
\end{align*}
